summary: Compare the best ecommerce accounting software for 2026. See how tools handle sales, payouts, fees, and growing transaction volume.
body_markdown:
The best ecommerce accounting software in 2026 combines a general ledger that fits the business with automation for sales, fees, refunds, and payouts across channels.


That setup matters as ecommerce grows. U.S. ecommerce sales reached[$340.2 billion in Q2 2026](https://www.census.gov/retail/mrts/www/data/pdf/ec_current.pdf) , up 12.2% year over year. More online sales also means more marketplace and payment processor data to account for, since orders are often grouped into payouts after fees and refunds are deducted. The ledger therefore needs the transaction detail behind each deposit.


This guide explains how to:


- compare seven accounting platforms by price and ecommerce fit;
- spot where general accounting software falls short with multi-channel data;
- choose automation for fees, payouts, and reconciliation before data reaches the ledger.


## **TL;DR**


- [Ecommerce accounting](https://synder.com/blog/ecommerce-accounting-best-practices/) has to record sales, payouts, fees, refunds, and timing differences that platform deposits combine into a single number.
- The right accounting system for ecommerce depends on transaction volume, the number of sales channels, entity structure, and reporting needs.
- General accounting platforms record what they receive, so payout matching, fee classification, and inventory costing need an automation layer between sales channels and the ledger.
- A trial with real payouts, refunds, and fees shows whether a platform fits before a migration starts.


## **What is ecommerce accounting software?**


Ecommerce accounting software is the system you use to keep track of what your online sales actually mean financially. It records revenue, expenses, and reports in a way that works with high order volume and platform-generated data.


In practice, this means working with sales data coming from ecommerce platforms, payment processors, and marketplaces, and recording that information in a way that produces accurate financial statements and ecommerce accounting reports. How that data gets into the system, whether manually or through integrations, varies by business and setup.


That basic setup works well on paper, but in practice, ecommerce accounting software often runs into limitations once real transaction data starts flowing in.


## **Limitations of ecommerce accounting software** ****


Ecommerce accounting software does a solid job recording financial data. The difficulty starts with how ecommerce data arrives. Sales do not come in as finished accounting entries. They arrive as pieces that need to be aligned before the numbers make sense, even in the best bookkeeping software for ecommerce.


It’s similar to unpacking deliveries from several couriers for a single order. Each box is labeled correctly, but none of them explains how everything fits together. Ecommerce accounting software stores the boxes. Someone still has to match them.


Ecommerce sellers make up nearly 40% of businesses seeking accounting automation, more than any other industry, according to Synder’s research of 1,000+ businesses. The challenges they raise fall into four gaps between platform data and the general ledger: payout matching, fee classification, refund timing, and inventory costing.


### **Payout-to-order matching gap**


A payout gap is the difference between the orders customers paid for and the single deposit that reaches the bank. Payment processors and marketplaces such as Shopify Payments, Stripe, PayPal, and Amazon group many orders into one payout, deduct their fees, and deposit the net amount days after the sales occurred. The bank feed shows one deposit with a date, an amount, and at most an ACH trace ID, with no order, fee, or refund detail behind it.


Closing the gap requires three-way matching: each order is tied to its payment processor transaction, and each group of transactions is tied to the bank deposit it produced. Shopify Payments assigns a payout ID and links it to each Shopify order ID, Stripe records a payout ID and a balance transaction for every charge, fee, and refund, and Amazon issues a settlement report (Flat File V2) for each settlement period, so the identifiers exist on the platform side. Through the bank feed alone, online retail accounting software receives only the deposit, and the identifiers reach the ledger only through an integration. In the same research, 33.6% of businesses named confusion over fees and payouts as an accounting challenge.


### **Fee and commission misclassification**


Platforms deduct fees before paying out, so a deposit recorded as sales understates revenue and leaves the fees out of the expense accounts. Common deductions include Amazon referral fees, FBA fulfillment fees, FBA monthly storage fees, Stripe processing fees, and PayPal transaction fees. Each deduction belongs in an expense account and the gross sale belongs in income, so one deposit has to be split into several entries.


Splitting deposits by hand is manual data entry, the most cited challenge in Synder’s research, named by 41.5% of businesses. An ecommerce bookkeeping automation tool performs the split by mapping each fee type to an account.


### **Refund, chargeback, and return matching**


Refunds, chargebacks, and returns follow different rules on each platform, and they can settle in a different payout than the original sale. A Shopify order paid out in one payout can be refunded weeks later, and[Shopify Payments deducts the refund](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shopify-payments/payouts/refunds) from the next available payout.[Stripe debits the disputed amount plus a dispute fee](https://support.stripe.com/questions/dispute-fees-faq) from the balance when a chargeback opens, and returns the disputed amount only if the dispute is won. Amazon reports refunds in the settlement report for the period in which they are processed, and standard seller accounts receive a settlement report every two weeks.


These timing differences mean a month’s deposits can differ from that month’s net sales even when every transaction is recorded correctly. Reconciliation issues were the third most cited challenge in Synder’s research, named by 30.4% of businesses. For sellers processing hundreds of refunds a month, accounting software for high transaction volumes has to link each refund to its original order and payout.


### **Inventory and COGS tracking disconnect**


Payment data carries prices and fees but not product costs, so cost of goods sold (COGS) cannot be calculated from deposits. Accurate COGS in accounting software for online retail business requires SKU-level quantities from every sale and return, matched to unit costs in the accounting system or an inventory tool. Each sale has to move cost from the Inventory Asset account to the Cost of Goods Sold account in QuickBooks Online or another ledger. Inventory held in Amazon fulfillment centers adds another source, the Amazon Inventory Ledger report, which has to agree with the quantities in the books.


Among retail and ecommerce businesses in Synder’s research, inventory and COGS tracking (44.7%) was cited almost as often as manual data entry (45.4%), a near-parity not seen in other industries. Sellers comparing the best inventory accounting software for ecommerce need to check whether product data reaches the ledger with each sale.


### **How Synder handles ecommerce accounting limitations**


[Synder](https://synder.com/industry/syndersync/) is an accounting automation platform that prepares ecommerce data before it is posted to the books, syncing sales, fees, refunds, payouts, and taxes from 30+ ecommerce and payment platforms into QuickBooks Online, Xero, NetSuite, Sage Intacct, and other accounting systems. It’s a San Francisco-based Y Combinator S21 company rated 4.7 across 3,400+ reviews.


#### **Payout matching with Per Transaction and Summary Sync**


Synder matches payouts to bank deposits through a clearing account that represents each payment platform in the books. In Per Transaction mode, Synder posts every sale, fee, and refund to the clearing account as a separate transaction with customer and product detail. In Summary Sync mode, Synder posts one journal entry per platform for each day, payout, or custom period, itemized by sales, fees, taxes, discounts, and refunds. In both modes, Synder records each payout as a transfer of the exact payout amount from the clearing account to the bank account, so the transfer matches the deposit on the QuickBooks Online Bank transactions page or in Xero bank reconciliation.


For Per Transaction users, Transaction Reconciliation matches every line in the clearing account to the platform’s own records, automated via API, standard upload, or custom mapping. Anything that doesn’t tie 100% is flagged, so you review only the transactions that need attention.


#### **Fee categorization mapped to your chart of accounts**


Synder records platform fees as expenses mapped to accounts in your existing chart of accounts, which keeps ecommerce automated bookkeeping consistent with the reports your accountant already uses. In Per Transaction mode, each processing fee posts as a separate expense tied to its sale. In Summary Sync mode, mapping groups split platform fees into separate lines, for example Amazon referral fees and FBA fulfillment fees, and each line is mapped to the account you choose.


#### **Balance checks before data is posted**


For Summary Sync users, Balance Reconciliation verifies that a period matches the platform’s reported starting and ending balances before summaries are posted to the books. Every reconciliation has a full audit trail you can download or revisit.

Middleware and order-management connectors move orders, inventory, and payments between storefronts and accounting systems. Native connectors built by accounting platforms, such as QuickBooks’ own Shopify and Stripe connectors, cover one sales channel each, and all-in-one bookkeeping platforms replace the ledger with their own.


Connecting several of these tools creates its own problem:[62% of finance teams reported integration issues](https://synder.com/downloadables/2025-emerging-trends-in-accounting-ai-progress-pitfalls-and-the-path-ahead/) when deploying automation, according to Synder’s 2025 survey of 424 U.S. finance leaders in ecommerce and SaaS. ### **How do ecommerce businesses handle payouts and fees in accounting?**


Ecommerce businesses typically receive payouts that combine multiple orders, fees, and refunds into a single bank deposit. Accounting software records these transactions, while ecommerce accounting solutions like Synder group sales by payout and post fees and refunds as separate entries, allowing deposits to be reconciled accurately and financial reports to remain clear.


### **Why don’t my bank deposits match my gross sales?**


Bank deposits don’t match gross sales because payment processors and marketplaces deduct fees, refunds, chargebacks, reserves, and withheld marketplace taxes before sending the payout. Amazon remits the marketplace facilitator tax it withholds, so that amount is recorded separately from the seller’s own sales tax payable. The deposit equals gross sales minus those deductions, and it can include sales from several days or from an earlier payout period. Tools that automate ecommerce bookkeeping break each deposit back into its components, posting gross sales to income and each deduction to its own account, so the payout total ties to the bank deposit.


### **How can ecommerce businesses reduce month-end close time?**


Ecommerce businesses reduce month-end close time by syncing transactions daily, matching payouts to deposits as they arrive, and leaving only flagged exceptions for review at month-end. Manual close work grows with every channel because each platform reports fees, refunds, and payout timing in its own format.[Healthy Meals Direct](https://synder.com/success-stories/healthy-meals-direct/) , which sells through Shopify and PayPal into QuickBooks Online, cut daily reconciliation from 3-4 hours to 30-45 minutes with Per Transaction sync and saves 70+ hours of manual work a month.


### **Should I import every order or use summary sync?**


Importing every order with Per Transaction sync gives order-level detail for audits, inventory, and product or customer reports, while Summary Sync keeps the ledger compact at high volume with one entry per platform per period. Per Transaction suits businesses that invoice from the ledger, track inventory there, or use classes and locations. Summary Sync suits businesses that use the ledger mainly for reconciliation and tax reporting. Synder offers both modes, and the mode is selected for each Synder organization.


### **Do ecommerce businesses need accounting automation software?**


Yes, while accounting software alone records data, ecommerce businesses often need accounting automation to manage high transaction volume and multiple sales channels. The best ecommerce accounting automation platforms help ensure sales, fees, taxes, and payouts are recorded consistently, reducing manual reconciliation and improving accuracy as the business scales.


### **How should I categorize Amazon fees, FBA fees, and Stripe fees in accounting software?**


Amazon referral fees, FBA fees, and Stripe fees each belong in a separate expense account in accounting software, so the cost of selling on each platform is visible in the profit and loss statement. A mapping that keeps these costs visible sends Amazon referral fees to a selling fees account, FBA fulfillment fees to a fulfillment or shipping expense account, FBA monthly storage fees to a warehousing expense account, and Stripe processing fees to a merchant fees account. Some businesses record FBA fulfillment fees in cost of goods sold instead, so the treatment should be confirmed with an accountant and applied consistently. Synder maps each fee type to the QuickBooks Online or Xero account you choose, through mapping groups in Summary Sync or fee expenses in Per Transaction mode.


### **Do ecommerce accounting platforms offer APIs?**


Major ecommerce accounting platforms offer APIs: QuickBooks Online has the QuickBooks Online Accounting API, Xero has the Xero Accounting API, NetSuite has SuiteTalk REST Web Services, and Sage Intacct has its Web Services API. Rate limits shape how fast data can move through these APIs, and Xero, for example, allows[60 calls per minute per organization](https://developer.xero.com/documentation/best-practices/api-call-efficiencies/rate-limits) and 1,000 to 5,000 calls per day depending on the app tier.
